title: Longitudinal associations among family function, psychological resilience, and frailty progression in older gastric cancer survivors: A random intercept cross‐lagged panel model
abstract: Abstract Objectives Older gastric cancer survivors after radical gastrectomy are vulnerable to frailty progression. Family function may influence frailty by enhancing individual psychological resilience. However, few studies have examined these longitudinal associations. We aimed to evaluate the longitudinal associations among family function, psychological resilience, and frailty. Methods A total of 412 older gastric cancer survivors who underwent radical gastrectomy were enrolled and assessed at hospital discharge, and again at 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively. Family function was assessed using the family adaptability and cohesion evaluation scale II, psychological resilience with the Connor–Davidson resilience scale, and frailty using the Tilburg frailty indicator. The random intercept cross‐lagged panel model was used to assess within‐ and between‐person longitudinal associations. Mediation effect analysis was conducted at the within‐person level. Results Family cohesion was indirectly associated with lower subsequent frailty through higher psychological resilience. The estimated indirect effects from T1 to T3 and from T2 to T4 were −.025 ( p = .012) and −.032 ( p = .004), respectively. While family adaptability was associated with psychological resilience at the between‐person level ( B = .707, p = .006), and psychological resilience was negatively associated with frailty ( B = −2.458, p = .003), the direct association between family adaptability and frailty was not significant ( B = −.097, p = .069). Conclusion Greater family cohesion was associated with lower subsequent frailty, with psychological resilience representing a potential pathway. These findings highlight the potential of resilience‐focused approaches to enhance the benefits of family support in addressing frailty.
